questions.prompt: A click listener on a form receives a bubbling click from a nested submit button. Why is this useful for delegation?

choices.text: The event propagates from the target through its ancestors.
The ancestor listener runs only because registration copies the listener to every child.
The event target changes to the form whenever propagation reaches the form listener.
A form receives descendant clicks only if it is also the element originally clicked.

questions.explanation: Bubbling carries the event along the ancestor path. It does not copy listeners or replace the original target with the current listener location.

questions.prompt: A cancelable link click is handled with `preventDefault()`. Which effect should be distinguished from propagation?

choices.text: The navigation is canceled and all later ancestor listeners are suppressed automatically.
The click stops propagating but the browser must still perform its normal navigation.
The call changes the link href so that subsequent unhandled clicks cannot navigate.
The navigation default action can be canceled while listeners still receive the event.

questions.explanation: preventDefault cancels a cancelable navigation default action. It neither stops propagation automatically nor edits the href attribute.

questions.prompt: A named text input is disabled when a form is submitted. What does the normal entry-construction algorithm do?

choices.text: It includes the value because disabled only prevents focus and editing, not submission.
It includes the value only when the disabled input also has the required attribute.
It omits that disabled control from the submitted entries.
It includes an empty string because disabled controls submit placeholders instead.

questions.explanation: Disabled controls are skipped during form entry construction. Neither a name nor required makes the disabled value submit; readonly has different semantics.

sources.claim: Form submission constructs entries from successful controls; disabled and unchecked controls are omitted and validation can be bypassed by specified APIs or attributes.

questions.prompt: An API receives data from a form with `required` and `type=email`. Which server assumption is valid?

choices.text: The server can trust submitted data because native validation runs for every client request.
The server must validate input even when the browser has native constraints.
The server needs checks for text fields but email fields enforce their format for all clients.
The server only validates fields without required because required implies trusted data.

questions.explanation: Native constraints improve client interaction but can be bypassed through submission paths or other clients. The server must validate all inputs it relies on.

questions.prompt: A bubbling event traverses parent and child elements. Which ordering is the propagation model built around?

choices.text: Capture toward the target, target handling, then bubbling outward.
Bubbling toward the target, target handling, then capture outward.
Target handling first, then capture toward the target, then bubbling outward.
Capture toward the target, bubbling outward, then target handling at the end.

questions.explanation: Capture travels toward the target and bubbling away from it for events that bubble. Not every event has a bubbling phase.

questions.prompt: A handler calls `preventDefault()` on an event whose `cancelable` property is false. What should the author expect?

choices.text: The call stops propagation even though it cannot cancel the browser default action.
The call changes cancelable to true and then prevents the default action.
The default action is canceled but the defaultPrevented property remains false.
That call cannot cancel the event default action.

questions.explanation: A noncancelable event cannot have its default action canceled by preventDefault. The call does not make it cancelable or stop propagation.

questions.prompt: A normal HTML form contains named controls. Which entry rules hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: An unchecked checkbox is normally omitted.
A readonly text control is omitted by the same rule as a disabled control.
Every button contributes its value regardless of submitter.
A disabled named input contributes its value because its name remains present.
A disabled text control is normally omitted.

questions.explanation: a: Only checked checkbox and radio controls contribute entries. b: Readonly does not impose the disabled submission exclusion. c: Submit buttons are included only when they are the submitter. d: Disabled controls are omitted even when they have a name. e: Entry construction skips disabled controls.
